definition: Multifaceted means having many different sides or aspects.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word multifaceted. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know multifaceted should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Restoring the old mill proved multifaceted work — part carpentry, part hydrology, part fundraising, and part town politics.
Two-sided grants exactly two aspects — every argument has that much — and stops far short of multifaceted.
Layered goes further than two-sided, stacking level on level, but it stops short of multifaceted, which opens onto many distinct sides at once.

Many-sided is the everyday phrasing for a thing with several aspects, and it stops at counting them. Multifaceted adds the gem's discipline: the many sides all belong to one object, distinct faces of a single whole. Many-sided notes the number; multifaceted keeps the sides attached to one thing.

Complex means made of interwoven parts that resist quick understanding — the difficulty lives in the tangling. Multifaceted only says one thing shows many distinct sides; those sides may each be simple. A multifaceted job can be four easy tasks; a complex problem knots its parts together.

One position, and a multifaceted one — four professions folded into a single badge.

Multifaceted is more precise than 'varied' because it keeps everything attached to one thing: a facet is one polished face of a single gem, so a multifaceted job, mind, or problem is one object turning many distinct sides toward you.
If the pieces do not belong to a whole, they are simply many — call them manifold instead.
Multifaceted is the boardroom-and-classroom word for one thing with many sides — a role, a crisis, a personality.
Keep the gem in mind to separate it from its unit-mates: multifaceted is one stone with many faces, manifold is many varied things, and complex adds that the parts tangle.
If you only mean 'complicated,' say that.

When Maple Falls hired a coordinator for its centennial, the council admitted up front that the position was multifaceted.
One week she was in the archives, checking dates for the history pageant; the next she was pricing tents and folding tables for the fairgrounds.
She scheduled the parade, recruited food vendors, and set up a booth where residents recorded memories of the old cannery.
None of the tasks was difficult on its own, and she often finished two in a morning.
What made the job remarkable was that permits, pageants, and oral histories were all sides of a single celebration, and she had to keep every side turning at once.
